content.title: Response to Reviewer J9kh
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and time dedicated to evaluating our work.

**Comment 1:** The performance isn't really that great overall, the method doesn't always beat comparators.

**Response 1:** We respectfully disagree that the performance is not great overall for not beating baselines at all tasks. We compare our method with lots of representative offline RL methods such as CQL, TD3-BC, and IQL, and current state-of-the-art methods such as PBRL, SAC-N, and EDAC. We have to emphasize that even if PBRL and SAC-N show a great success, they did not beat other methods in all the environments. In our paper, BURL achieves better performance in 11/15 tasks and obtains a great improvement in parametric efficiency, as shown in Fig.2 and Table 3. 

**Comment 2:** On the Mujoco environments, there's not much of a gain in the number of ensembles, and it's only a factor of 2 over EDAC?

**Response 2:** As illustrated in Fig. 2, BURL needs 2~5 ensembles in halfcheetah and walker2d tasks, which is half of the ensembles that EDAC needs; in the hopper task, BURL needs only one-tenth of ensembles of EDAC, which should not be ignored. 

Moreover, BURL is based on SAC-N and PBRL. Compared with SAC-N and PBRL, BURL shows a large improvement in parametric efficiency. As presented in Table 3, BURL requires only half or even one percent of the parameters for PBRL or SAC-N. In conclusion, BURL can achieve favorable performance with fewer ensembles and exhibit better computational efficiency.

**Comment 3:** The OOD term doesn't seem to add much value according to the ablation studies. The OOD term doesn't seem to add much (1/2 works better).

**Response 3:** We thank the reviewer for pointing out this issue. In our paper, we propose the repulsive regularization term by sampling OOD actions to improve the diversity among Q-values. To present the importance of the OOD term, we add experiments on 9 tasks. All the other settings are the same, except for not using the OOD term for updating the Q-networks. We put the comparison and analysis in Appendix C.

| Environments    | w/o OOD term |  with OOD term  |
| :-------------- | :----------: | :-------------: |
| halfcheetah-m   |     70.6     | 69.2 $\pm$ 2.7  |
| halfcheetah-m-r |     66.6     | 66.7 $\pm$ 2.0  |
| halfcheetah-m-e |     11.8     | 104.2 $\pm$ 2.4 |
| walker2d-m      |     -0.1     | 95.1 $\pm$ 2.7  |
| walker2d-m-r    |     17.7     | 96.1 $\pm$ 2.3  |
| walker2d-m-e    |     2.1      | 112.4 $\pm$ 1.1 |
| hopper-m        |     1.0      | 102.0 $\pm$ 1.2 |
| hopper-m-r      |    103.2     | 102.9 $\pm$ 1.1 |
| hopper-m-e      |     15.5     | 112.3 $\pm$ 1.8 |

We remark that this result is consistent with Fig. 5. In hopper-medium-replay, halfcheetah-medium, and halfcheetah-medium-replay tasks, optimizing ensemble BNNs without OOD diversity regularization is sufficient to obtain competitive performance. In the other tasks, given a few ensembles, the OOD diversity regularization term is necessary for favorable performance. Therefore, we suggest that the OOD diversity term is useful for our method.

**Comment 4:** The paper isn't always very clear.

**Response 4:** We added a summary of our contributions in the Introduction and some guiding descriptions in Section 3 to clarify the structure. If you have any further questions or suggestions about the clarity and quality, we would be more than happy to answer them in the next revision.

**Comment 5:** while the paper presents interesting ideas, there are no concrete theorems to justify it.

**Response 5:** Thanks for the comment, but we cannot fully agree that there are no concrete theorems to justify our idea. As suggested in Section 3.1 and Appendix A, our work is mainly based on the linear MDP setting and the LSVI algorithm and approximates the Bayesian posterior of the value function. We show Theorem 1 to relate the uncertainty quantification of Q-values to the standard deviation of the posterior distribution. This enables better uncertainty quantification and a less conservative estimation of Q-values for OOD actions. The empirical results also validate our algorithm. We also add the relational descriptions and propositions in Appendix A.

When incorporated with ensemble modeling, they show that their proposed methods have competitive performance with the SOTA method SAC-N which requires a large amount of computations as N is large. They also show that the number of parameters in their model is smaller than PBRL (1.5M vs 2.9M) and SAC-N (1.5M vs 135.8M for N=500).

content.title: Response to Reviewer AtQJ
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and time dedicated to evaluating our work.

**Comment 1:** Besides the repulsive force term, everything else is pretty incremental.

**Response 1:** We respectfully disagree that our work is incremental. In our paper, we propose a lightweight uncertainty quantification method by replacing the last layer of the ensemble critic network with BNNs, which forms an approximate Bayesian posterior of the value function. Such a modification provides reliable uncertainty for pessimistic learning and performs better than previous uncertainty-based work with fewer ensembles. To improve the diversity among samples from ensembles and BNNs, we introduce the repulsive regularization term by explicitly maximizing the uncertainty of Q-values for OOD actions. We add a summary in the Introduction to clarify our contributions.

**Comment 2:** BURL still needs ensemble modeling, and the abstract is misleading.

**Response 2:** We thank the reviewer for pointing out this issue. Our algorithm does need a few ensembles to obtain reliable uncertainty quantification and competitive performance compared to other SOTA methods. We modify the abstract and the Introduction to clarify our contributions.

For BURL, we find that using no more than 5 networks is sufficient to obtain strong performance in most tasks. In contrast, previous uncertainty-based offline RL algorithms require a large number of ensembles for competitive performance. For example, SAC-N, which achieves state-of-the-art performance in Gym-Mujoco tasks, requires 500 ensembles in hopper environments. We show the parametric efficiency in Table 3, where BURL performs better than other methods. The SOTA algorithm EDAC also needs much more ensembles than our method, as shown in Fig. 2. In walker2d and hopper tasks, EDAC needs 10 or 50 ensembles, while our method requires 5 or fewer ensembles.

**Response 3:** As stated in Section 3.1 and Appendix A, our work focuses on the linear MDP setting and is based on Least-Square Value Iteration (LSVI) [1] algorithm. By assuming that the transition dynamics and the reward function are linear in a representation $\phi(s,a)$, the value function $Q(s,a)$ is also linear in $\phi(s,a)$, as shown in Assumption 1. This assumption is widely accepted and used in previous work [2][3][4].

In our work, we consider a Bayesian perspective of LSVI and learn the posterior distribution of the Q-function. Under the linear MDP assumption, we can relate the standard deviation of the estimated posterior distribution $\mathbb{P}(\tilde{Q}|s,a,\mathcal{D}_m)$ to the lower confidence bound penalty, which is used to enforce the pessimism in other works [3][5]. The detailed proof for Theorem 1 is shown in Appendix A.2.

[1] Osband et al., Generalization and exploration via randomized value functions, ICML 2016

[2] Jin et al., Provably Efficient Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation, COLT 2020

[3] Jin et al., Is Pessimism Provably Efficient for Offline RL? ICML 2021

[4] Agarwal et al., Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Algorithms (2022)

[5] Bai et al., Pessimistic Bootstrapping for Uncertainty-Driven Offline Reinforcement Learning, ICLR 2022

**Comment 4:** How is the performance of Q-ensemble model (e.g. PBRL model) would be if it is trained with our loss functions instead of their own loss function? And is the Bayesian inference module necessary or not?

**Response 4:** We thank the reviewer for pointing out this interesting problem. As stated in section 3.3, the loss function Eq. (8) is computed based on all the n*M sampled Q-values of the ensemble BNNs and contains three parts: pessimistic updates on in-distribution data, KL divergence, and OOD diversity term. While the loss function of PBRL contains pessimistic updates on both in-distribution data and OOD data, it is hard to work by directly replacing loss functions. Moreover, pessimistic updates on OOD data are necessary for PBRL. Therefore, we conduct the following experiments and add the comparisons and the analysis in Appendix D.3.

We first illustrate that other methods (e.g. PBRL) cannot perform well with fewer ensembles but may benefit from the OOD repulsive term. In practice, we choose PBRL as the basis and add comparisons with 1) PBRL with fewer ensembles and 2) PBRL with fewer ensembles and OOD diversity loss. Experimental results are shown as follows. The first comparison illustrates that PBRL with fewer ensembles cannot achieve the same performance as BURL. And the second comparison shows that PBRL may benefit from the OOD diversity loss but is still inferior to BURL. This result shows that the Bayesian inference module is necessary, and the OOD repulsive term may be useful for other ensemble-based methods.

content.title: Response to Reviewer AtQJ (follow-up)
content.comment:
**Comment 5:** “These methods lack specific uncertainty estimation and lead to overly conservative behavior.” This is quite unfair, e.g. PBRL does have provable uncertainty estimation and works pretty good in practice.

**Response 5:** We have rewritten this paragraph in the preliminaries to prevent misunderstanding. In this part, we first list offline RL methods which constrain the learned policy (e.g. BCQ) or penalize the OOD values (e.g. CQL). These methods (BCQ or CQL) lack uncertainty estimation and may cause overly conservative behavior. In contrast, PBRL and EDAC do have better uncertainty estimation and perform better than policy constraint methods (e.g. BCQ) or value regularization methods (e.g. CQL). Our algorithm is also an uncertainty-based offline RL method, while PBRL and EDAC are the main baselines for comparisons. The empirical results in Table 1 illustrate that our algorithm performs better than PBRL or EDAC in most tasks with fewer ensembles.

**Comment 6:** Why handling OOD actions only via this term would give that good performance?

**Response 6:** We thank the reviewer for pointing out this issue. We remark that good performance comes from two designs: the Bayesian posterior and the OOD repulsive term. In our work, we propose to use BNNs to provide uncertainty quantification, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Then to improve the efficiency and enforce the diversity between different posterior samples, a repulsive regularization term is introduced. We added experiments to figure out the necessity of BNNs and the OOD repulsive term, as shown in Table 5 and Appendix D.3.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a model-free offline RL approach which incorporates a Bayesian posterior estimation for uncertainty quantification into the Q-network. The model consists of a network to learn the representations of state-action pairs and an approximate Bayesian inference in the last layer, which together with repulsive regularization are used in an ensemble learning scheme for diversification. Experiments on D4RL benchmark data show that the proposed work archives competitive performance compared to several baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ The idea of estimating the lower confidence bound of value estimates within the Q-network is interesting and somewhat novel.
+ The experiments are extensive and reproducible, and the results are promising on the D4RL benchmark data.

Weaknesses:
- The writing of the paper can be largely improved. 
- The significance and impact of contributions are not very clear.
- Some of the claims in the paper are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
+ The approach seems to be reproducible and some practical implications are presented.

- The clarity of the paper in terms of structure, contributions, approach, and argumentation should be improved. Some notations should be modified/clarified (e.g., E1. 1 and Eq. 7). Some concepts/arguments are introduced and not used later in the approach.

- It is difficult to assess the technical quality of the paper due to the clarity issue. However, it seems that some parts regarding the Q-learning method are incorrect to some extent. For instance, Eq. 1 is not a Q update as it does not include a 'max' operation. In general, Q-learning is not considered a linear approach, and in case of offline data, should use importance sampling. Also, it is not clear why the authors focus on Q-learning in the first place and not other techniques.

- Accordingly, it seems that the approach is more of a behavioral cloning algorithm as the network learns a representation \phi which is utilized in a (linear) regression task. To me, \phi(s,a).w is not equivalent to the Q-values. Could you elaborate further and clarify the RL updates in the optimization process?

- The authors motivate their approach as opposed to ensemble learning at the beginning and claim they propose a lightweight uncertainty estimation. However, they benefit from an ensemble of models for uncertainty estimation in their framework, together with Bayesian inference. Although they show in the experiment that they need 'fewer' models in the ensemble than competitors, the claim is not well supported in my view, particularly that the results are not completely agreeing with this as well.

- Subsequently, there are other methods, either model-free such as UWAC [1] or model-based like COMBO [2] that propose approaches that do not require ensembles for uncertainty quantification (both are mentioned in the related work). I would suggest to include a comparison (technical and empirical) with such techniques, especially UWAC.

- As I understood, the uncertainty, at the end, is quantified via ensembling and min Q-value, rather than the standard deviation introduced in Theorem 1. Could you clarify whether this is the case and why?

- When sampling OOD actions from the current policy, how do you ensure that it falls out of the data support?

- It seems that the results reported for some methods (e.g., I checked for MOPO) are different from the results introduced in their paper. Could you clarify what is the reason? Have you recalculated the scores? If yes, how the settings are different that led to different outcome?

- I also suggest to include other methods in the comparison. There are many model-based and model-free offline RL techniques on the same benchmark data and the results can be directly taken from their corresponding paper. A comparison with those would be helpful.


[1] Wu et al., Uncertainty Weighted Actor-Critic for Offline Reinforcement Learning (2021)
[2] Yu et al., Combo: Conservative offline model-based policy optimization (2021)

However, the significance/impact of contributions are limited on the field and the paper should be improved in terms of clarity and technical quality/correctness. I hence vote for a reject.

content.title: Response to Reviewer w9ZG
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and time dedicated to evaluating our work.

**Comment 1:** The significance and impact of contributions are not very clear.

**Response 1:** Thanks for your suggestion. We add a summary of the contribution at the end of the Introduction. Our contribution can be three-fold: **1)** We propose BURL, a lightweight uncertainty-based offline RL algorithm that uses last-layer BNN to approximate the Bayesian posterior with the help of a few ensembles. We relate the Bayesian uncertainty to the LCB penalty in linear MDP settings. **2)** We introduce a repulsive regularization term to improve the diversity among different posterior samples, leading to better parametric efficiency. **3)** We conduct a large number of experiments and ablation studies to validate our algorithm, which shows competitive performance and reasonable uncertainty quantification. 

**Comment 2:** Structure, notations, and arguments should be clarified.

**Response 2:** We add guiding descriptions and several subtitles in Section 3 to clearly present the structure. In Section 3, we first introduce the Bayesian posterior for uncertainty quantification and relate it to the LCB penalty. Since the LCB penalty cannot be directly applied to environments with high-dimensional observations, we approximate the LCB-term via the Bayesian posterior of the non-linear neural networks. As shown in Fig. 1, we consider the representation $\phi(s, a)$ as the output of hidden layers of the Q-network and $w$ as the weight of the last layer. To perform uncertainty estimation and Bayesian inference, we sample Q-values from the posterior distribution and ensemble BNNs. To further improve the computational efficiency, we propose the repulsive force for regularization and improve the diversity in different posterior samples. Finally, we give the concrete optimization objective and algorithmic descriptions for BURL.

We have rewritten the backgrounds about Eq. (1) in the preliminaries and added more explanations for Eq. (7) to improve clarity.

**Comment 3:** Eq. (1) is not a Q update as it does not include a 'max' operation.

We respectfully disagree that Eq. (1) is not a Q update and agree that Q-learning includes a 'max' operation. However, the explicit 'max' operation by selecting the action corresponding to the maximum Q-value is only suitable in discrete action spaces. In our paper, we consider tasks in D4RL datasets with continuous action spaces. Therefore, we express the 'argmax' by defining the policy network $\pi(\cdot|s)$ that acts greedily with respect to the Q-function with entropy regularization. In calculating the best next action in Eq. (1), we sample actions from the policy $a\sim \pi(\cdot|s)$, which is standard in online and offline RL algorithms for continuous actions. The policy (actor) is trained to maximize the Q-values, as described in Eq. (9).

**Comment 4:** Q-learning is not considered a linear approach.

**Response 4:** We thank the reviewer for pointing out the ambiguity problem. Our method is based on Least-Square Value Iteration (LSVI) [1][2], which is a classic Q-learning style algorithm in linear MDPs. In linear MDP settings, LSVI can obtain a closed-form solution because the value function $Q(s, a)$ is linear with respect to the representation $\phi(s, a)$, as discussed in Appendix A.1. We have modified the preliminaries and added further introduction about LSVI in Section A of the appendix. We remark that the linear MDP assumption based on the LSVI algorithm is widely accepted and used in the theoretical analysis for online and offline RL [3][4][5].

[1] Bradtke et al., Linear least-squares algorithms for temporal difference learning, Machine Learning 1996

[2] Osband et al., Generalization and exploration via randomized value functions, ICML 2016

[3] Jin et al., Provably Efficient Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation, COLT 2020

[4] Jin et al., Is Pessimism Provably Efficient for Offline RL? ICML 2021

[5] Agarwal et al., Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Algorithms (2022)

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer w9ZG

content.title: Response to Reviewer w9ZG (follow-up)
content.comment:
**Comment 5:** In case of offline data, Q-learning should use importance sampling.

**Response 5:** We respectfully disagree that Q-learning should use importance sampling since the TD target of the Q-function is $r_{t+1}+\gamma Q(s_{t+1}, a')$ where actions $a'$ are sampled from $\pi(\cdot|s)$ and have nothing to do with the behavior policy. 

Although Q-learning style methods can be directly applied in offline RL, it is well-known that using off-policy RL methods suffers from the distributional shift with limited data. Our method belongs to uncertainty-based offline RL algorithms, which estimate the uncertainty of Q-values for OOD actions and obtain less conservative estimation than policy constraint methods (e.g. BCQ, BEAR) or value regularization methods (e.g. CQL). We also remark that, if the offline dataset has sufficient diversity and contains a large amount of data, the Q-learning based algorithm like QR-DQN [1] can obtain similar results compared to online training.

[1] Agarwal R, Schuurmans D, Norouzi M. An optimistic perspective on offline reinforcement learning, ICML 2020

**Comment 6:**  The approach is more of a behavioral cloning algorithm as the network learns a representation $\phi$ which is utilized in a (linear) regression task. And $\phi(s,a)^\text{T}w$ is not equivalent to the Q-values?

**Response 6:** We thank the reviewer for pointing out this problem. We insist that our method does not perform behavioral cloning since the representation $\phi(s,a)$ is learned by regressing the (pessimistic) target Q-value rather than the behavior policy. As a result, our method is inherently different from the policy constraint-based algorithms that enforce the learned policy to be close to the behavior policy.

In liner MDPs, we assume that the transition dynamics and the reward function are linear in a feature mapping $\phi$. Then, according to the previous theoretical results [1], we have the following corollary: For a linear MDP, for any policy $\pi$, there exist weights $[\textbf{w}^\pi_h]_{h\in[H]}$ such that for any $(s,a,h)\in \mathcal{S}\times \mathcal{{A}}\times [H]$, we have $Q_h^\pi(s,a)=<\phi(s,a),\textbf{w}_h^\pi>$. We refer to [1] for more discussion, and such an assumption is widely accepted and used in previous works. We add relative descriptions in Section A of the appendix.

As illustrated in Fig. 1, the critic network can be separated into hidden layers and the last layer. While the hidden layers output the representation of state-action pairs, we use Bayesian neural networks in the last layer to provide the posterior of the value function and uncertainty quantification. In our approach, the critic loss in Eq. (8) is used to train the parameter of the last layer and also the representation $\phi(s,a)$. In practice, we use a SAC-style framework to simultaneously update the critic and the actor.

[1] Jin et al., Provably Efficient Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation, COLT 2020

**Comment 7:** Does Bayesian inference still need ensembles?

**Response 7:**  Yes. To obtain the competitive performance compared to other SOTA algorithms, we still need a few ensemble networks to obtain reliable uncertainty quantification. We remark that in most of the tasks, we find using no more than 5 networks is sufficient to obtain strong performance. In contrast, previous uncertainty-based offline RL algorithms require a large number of ensembles for competitive performance. For example, SAC-N, which achieves state-of-the-art performance in Gym-Mujoco tasks, requires 500 ensembles in hopper environments. We show the parametric efficiency in Table 3, where BURL performs better than other methods. The SOTA algorithm EDAC also needs much more ensembles than our method, as shown in Fig. 2. In walker2d and hopper tasks, EDAC needs 10 or 50 ensembles, while our method requires 5 or fewer ensembles.

content.title: Response to Reviewer w9ZG (follow-up)
content.comment:
**Comment 8:** Comparisons with UWAC and COMBO.

**Response 8:** We thank the reviewer for pointing out further comparisons with UWAC and COMBO. UWAC uses Monte Carlo dropout to estimate the uncertainty, while still requiring policy constraints for regularization. COMBO combines offline model-based methods with value regularization, which is very different from our method that quantifies the uncertainty of Q-values for state-action pairs. In our experiments, we compare our method with state-of-the-art uncertainty-based methods such as PBRL, SAC-N, and EDAC, and the model-free offline RL methods such as CQL, TD3-BC, and IQL, as well as the model-based method MOPO.

We add the comparisons and analyses in Section D.1 of the appendix. 

| Environments    |      UWAC       |      COMBO      |      BURL       |
| :-------------- | :-------------: | :-------------: | :-------------: |
| halfcheetah-r   |  2.3 $\pm$ 0.0  | 38.8 $\pm$ 3.7  | 30.9 $\pm$ 1.1  |
| halfcheetah-m   | 42.2 $\pm$ 0.4  | 54.2 $\pm$ 1.5  | 69.2 $\pm$ 2.7  |
| halfcheetah-m-r | 35.9 $\pm$ 3.7  | 55.1 $\pm$ 1.0  | 66.7 $\pm$ 2.0  |
| halfcheetah-m-e | 42.7 $\pm$ 0.3  | 90.0 $\pm$ 5.6  | 104.2 $\pm$ 2.4 |
| halfcheetah-e   | 92.9 $\pm$ 0.6  |        -        | 107.1 $\pm$ 2.6 |
| walker2d-r      |  2.0 $\pm$ 0.4  |  7.0 $\pm$ 3.6  |  7.4 $\pm$ 5.7  |
| walker2d-m      | 75.4 $\pm$ 3.0  | 81.9 $\pm$ 2.8  | 95.1 $\pm$ 2.7  |
| walker2d-m-r    | 23.6 $\pm$ 6.9  | 56.0 $\pm$ 8.6  | 96.1 $\pm$ 2.3  |
| walker2d-m-e    | 96.5 $\pm$ 9.1  | 103.3 $\pm$ 5.6 | 112.4 $\pm$ 1.1 |
| walker2d-e      | 108.4 $\pm$ 0.4 |        -        | 112.5 $\pm$ 0.5 |
| hopper-r        |  2.7 $\pm$ 0.3  | 17.9 $\pm$ 1.4  | 27.9 $\pm$ 7.8  |
| hopper-m        | 50.9 $\pm$ 4.4  | 97.2 $\pm$ 2.2  | 102.0 $\pm$ 1.2 |
| hopper-m-r      | 25.3 $\pm$ 1.7  | 89.5 $\pm$ 1.8  | 102.9 $\pm$ 1.1 |
| hopper-m-e      | 44.9 $\pm$ 8.1  | 111.1 $\pm$ 2.9 | 112.3 $\pm$ 1.8 |
| hopper-e        | 110.5 $\pm$ 0.5 |        -        | 111.4 $\pm$ 1.2 |

We remark that there exist differences between the 'v0' and 'v2' of Mujoco environments in D4RL datasets. While almost all the methods are evaluated on 'v2' datasets, the original paper of UWAC reports results on 'v0' datasets. Therefore, we adopt the reimplementation results of UWAC and perform comparisons with the same criterion.

**Comment 9:** The difference between the min Q-value and the standard deviation to estimate the uncertainty.

**Response 9:** As stated in the last paragraph of Section 3.1, we discuss two methods to estimate the pessimistic value function: **1)** calculating the standard deviation of the posterior as LCB penalty $Q_{\text{lcb}}^1=\bar{Q}(s_t,a_t)-\alpha \Gamma_t(s_t,a_t)$, where $\bar{Q}(s_t,a_t)$ indicates the mean Q-value and $\Gamma_t^{\text{lcb}}=\phi(s_t,a_t)^\text{T}\Sigma_w\phi(s_t,a_t).$ **2)** taking the minimal value of the Q-samples from the posterior distribution $Q_{\text{lcb}}^2(s_t,a_t)=\min_{k\in[n]}Q^{(k)}(s_t,a_t)$. We show that these two kinds of pessimism are approximately equivalent under Gaussian assumption, as shown in Eq. (5) in our paper and Eq. (3) in [1].

We choose $Q_{\text{lcb}}^2$ for two reasons: **1)** it is easy to combine with ensemble methods by sampling multiple values from both the ensemble and BNNs; **2)** the sampling method can be calculated effectively via matrix manipulation by using multiple noise vectors as inputs.

[1] An et al., Uncertainty-based offline reinforcement learning with diversified q-ensemble, NeurIPS 2021

content.title: Response to Reviewer w9ZG (follow-up)
content.comment:
**Comment 10:** How to ensure OOD actions by sampling from the current policy.

**Response 10:** We thank the reviewer for pointing out this interesting issue. In general, we can roughly regard any actions that are far from behavior policies as OOD actions. Since behavior policy is unknown, we can only generate OOD actions by sampling from some distributions that are different from the behavior policy. We consider two ways to generate OOD actions: randomly sampling from the action space or the learned policy. 

As shown in Eq. (1), the Q-value of the state-action pair $Q(s,a)$ is updated by regressing the target $E[r+\gamma Q(s',a')]$, where $Q(s',a')$ is often inaccurate in the offline setting since $a'$ can be OOD actions chosen by the learned policy. As a result, we suggest that sampling OOD actions from the learned policy leads to better pessimism for the neighbor field of the learned policy. 
In addition, we find that randomly sampling OOD actions in the action space is insufficient to enforce pessimism. We add experiments to compare the different OOD sampling methods and the results are given as follows. We find random sampling OOD actions causes overestimation and final divergence of the value function in halfcheetah and walker tasks. We put the comparison and analysis in Section D.2 of the appendix. 
| Environments    | random sampling from the action space | sampling from the learned policy |
| :-------------- | :------------------------------------------: | :-------------------------------------: |
| halfcheetah-m   |                                         0.5 |                         69.2 $\pm$ 2.7 |
| halfcheetah-m-r |                                         1.1 |                         66.7 $\pm$ 2.0 |
| halfcheetah-m-e |                                        -1.9 |                        104.2 $\pm$ 2.4 |
| walker2d-m      |                                        -0.3 |                         95.1 $\pm$ 2.7 |
| walker2d-m-r    |                                         6.9 |                         96.1 $\pm$ 2.3 |
| walker2d-m-e    |                                        -0.3 |                        112.4 $\pm$ 1.1 |
| hopper-m        |                                        30.5 |                        102.0 $\pm$ 1.2 |
| hopper-m-r      |                                        99.9 |                        102.9 $\pm$ 1.1 |
| hopper-m-e      |                                        14.1 |                        112.3 $\pm$ 1.8 |

**Comment 11:** The results of MOPO are different from the results in their paper.

**Response 11:** In our experiments, all comparisons in the Gym-Mujoco domain are conducted on the newest 'v2' datasets. As presented in  http://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/datasets/offline_rl/, the 'v2' version was released on Jul 2, 2021. However, MOPO was published in NeurIPS 2020, and their paper performs experiments on the 'v0' datasets. That is the reason why the reported results in our paper are different from the results in their paper. 

Since currently most methods are evaluated on 'v2' datasets, we choose the same criterion and compare our method with other approaches based on the same datasets. We cite the reproduced results of MOPO from [1]. We do not recalculate the scores or use different experimental settings.

[1] Bai et al., Pessimistic Bootstrapping for Uncertainty-Driven Offline Reinforcement Learning, ICLR 2022

**Comment 12:** More comparisons with other methods using their reported results.

**Response 12:** Since our method mainly focuses on uncertainty quantification, we compare it with the SOTA uncertainty-based offline RL methods, including PBRL (ICLR 2022), SAC-N (NeurIPS 2021), and EDAC (NeurIPS 2021), which has been proved to outperform previous popular methods, including REM (ICML 2020), BEAR (NeurIPS 2019), BRAC, MoReL (NeurIPS 2020), UWAC (ICML 2020), and CQL (NeurIPS 2020). In our experiments, we show that our method performs better than PBRL, SAC-N, and EDAC with fewer ensembles. Moreover, in Section 5, we also compare our method with many representative model-free algorithms, including CQL, TD3-BC (NeurIPS 2021), IQL (ICLR 2022), and ATAC (ICML 2022). We also compare BURL with the model-based algorithm MOPO (NeurIPS 2020) and add comparisons with UWAC and COMBO (NeurIPS 2021) in the appendix.
